utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Kasagic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will begin, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Kasagic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if it was the fact that the witness spoke very quietly or his microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you just say a few words, Mr. Kasagic, so that we can check whether the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. I can hear everything now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Fine. Please proceed. Perhaps you could take care that you are not too far away from the microphones. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, during the course of your testimony earlier, you referred to some of the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff and an occasion on which the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff were put to the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina for verification. You indicated, if I recall correctly, that on that occasion you objected to the decisions, or to a decision, and that three other people did as well. The Court made reference to the possibility of obtaining any documentation that might relate to verification of ARK Crisis Staff decisions by the Assembly, and I think we have at least one such document that bears on that issue, and I'll be presenting that to you in a moment. Let me ask you first, however, if the -- you referred to a specific decision. Was it that specific decision that was up for verification, or was it a host of ARK Crisis Staff decisions that were presented to the Assembly for verification or rejection?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly was supposed to confirm or reject all decisions issued by the Crisis Staff in the meantime, in the interim, up to the sitting of the Assembly. But the reason I remember this particular decision is that I was deeply opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall who, in addition to the Assembly delegates, was present on that occasion? And specifically, do you recall the presence of various republic-level and regional figures?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that no one from the republic level was present. As for the regional level, this was a regional Assembly. In the meantime, I recalled that Marinko Kontic voted in the same way as I did, against this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was this the kind of Assembly where issues other than the possible verification of ARK Crisis Staff decisions were raised? For example, where there were briefings about the political and security situation in the region or in the republic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the contents of the discussion at that Assembly. All I recall is this decision, which I opposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at the meeting of the ARK Assembly on July 17th, 1992. That can be found in the binder at tab 26. Mr. Kasagic, tab 26 contains the extract from the minutes of the 18th Session of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, held in the great hall of the cultural centre, commencing at 1100 hours. As you can see from the agenda on the first page, item number 4 was the verification of the decisions and conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff and War Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Now, it's correct, is it not, Mr. Kasagic, that the previous session of the Assembly of the autonomous region had been held back in April of 1992, that is, the one immediately preceding this one?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't recall the other sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does that generally conform to your recollection of the lapse between the Assembly -- the meeting of the Assembly at roughly the beginning of the war and then the next meeting after the conflict began? I see you nodding your head, but you'll have to answer audibly.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay a lot of attention to the work of the Assembly of the ARK Krajina. I felt that this was a community of municipalities. When the war began, it somehow lost its meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. The simple question was whether the lapse of time of approximately three months, whether that is consistent with your memory. If so, please tell us. If not, then -- or if you don't know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Looking quickly at item 4, the verification of the decisions and conclusions adopted by the Crisis Staff and War Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the minutes indicate that there was a debate in which several Assembly members took part, and that all the decisions and conclusions were verified; that of the 99 Assembly members present, 98 voted in favour of the decisions and conclusions and one Assembly member was against the decisions and conclusions of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did notice that, yes. I see that it says so here, but that's not correct, because I recall that four of us voted against.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you've indicated that there was a great deal you didn't recall about the Assembly and that you didn't pay much attention, but perhaps I can direct your attention to certain portions of the minutes that may jog your recollection. First of all, if we could look at the indications of attendance that precedes the listing of the agenda items. We see here that the session was attended by a number of persons who were not members of the Assembly, including Minister of Defence Subotic, Velibor Ostojic, the republic minister of information; Dragan Kalinic, the republic health minister of RS; General Talic; Milan Martic, the minister of the interior of the SRK; and Goran Hadzic, among others. Mr. Kasagic, does that refresh your recollection about the attendance of a number of dignitaries from both the republic level and from outside RS at this session of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall those persons. I was obsessed with this decision, which was very wrong, and I concentrated on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We also see that under item 1, Mr. Brdjanin, the president of the War Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and Stojan Zupljanin, who was the secretary of the Secretariat of the Interior and chief of the security services centre of the ARK, gave reports on the current political and security situation in the ARK, and that General Talic and Zivorad Ninkovic and Mr. Martic advised the Assembly members of the military operations of the VRS in the Posavina. Can you tell us anything about the reports given by Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Zupljanin, General Talic, Ninkovic, or Martic on the occasion of this Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't recall. It's been a long time. I don't remember anything else apart from this decision, because I've talked about it so often and I also had the Official Gazette number 5 of the ARK Krajina, which published that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you raise objections to any other decision by the ARK Crisis Staff other than the one that you've emphasised during the course of your direct examination here in Court?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on good terms with Brdjanin. I did not agree with him, and I was often in conflict with him because of the things he was doing which were detrimental to us. But I did not attend sessions of the ARK Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, the question was quite simple: Whether you objected to any other decision than you mentioned in your testimony in chief where you specifically - and you repeated it this morning - expressed your disagreement with one decision. So was there -- did you raise any objection during the meeting, during this Assembly meeting, against any other decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to ask that this -- that tab 26 be given a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P990, Your Honours, and the English translation P990.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I can't recall offhand if you indicated one way or another during your direct examination, but did you attend meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, no. This session is the one I remember. But certainly not the Crisis Staff, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were aware, however, that presidents of municipalities within the Autonomous Region of Krajina did attend Crisis Staff meetings, that is, meetings of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, if I may, to a press article from Glas dated June 9th, 1992, which is located at tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, that will also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 25 will be P991, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll give you a moment to look at that, Mr. Kasagic, but I'll indicate to you I'll be directing your attention to the second paragraph after the heading, "Banja Luka, June 9th," which reflects a remark by Mr. Brdjanin. First of all, that second paragraph, which begins with the words "I am amazed at this assessment by Kasagic," appears to reflect the tension between you and Mr. Brdjanin that you referred to earlier. But what I wanted specifically to direct your attention to was the third sentence of that paragraph, in which Mr. Brdjanin states: "Secondly, at every meeting of our Crisis Staff, which is held every Monday, all presidents of municipal crisis staffs are present and everything is discussed in full detail, and clearly."

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you -- I presume you read this article on June 9th, because it dealt, in part, with your relationship with Brdjanin. Do you recall reading it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does seeing that article now, whether for the first time or again after a lapse of some years, refresh your recollection that presidents of municipal crisis staffs attended the regular meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This does not assist me, because I never knew they attended the Crisis Staff. I only saw Brdjanin in all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could have just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I was a little surprised to hear you insist so emphatically that you never attended any meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff. Let me direct your attention to an interview which you referred to in your examination-in-chief with the Office of the Prosecutor that was conducted on July 20th, 2001. I'm not going to ask you if you recall that, because you referred to it in your examination-in-chief. That's located at tab 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that will need an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, the document in front of you, I realise, is in English. There is no B/C/S translation, so I will read out slowly the relevant passage so that you can understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I take it that for the Defence, at least, the audiotape is available so that they can check all of the context? Because Mr. Krajisnik might not be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, for your information, if there's any need, the audiotape is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's a subject again I may return to later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at page 13 of that translation, the question was asked: "You said that you attended at least one ARK Crisis Staff ... how many ARK Crisis Staff meetings did you attend?" Answer: "Only that one occasion." And then you proceeded to indicate -- well, let me leave it with that. Does that refresh your memory now, Mr. Kasagic, about your attendance at an ARK Crisis Staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what I said, the session I attended, as far as I can remember, was not a session of the Crisis Staff of the ARK Krajina; it was the staff that was established after the SOS was established, and it was Predrag Radic who was the president of that Crisis Staff, not Brdjanin. But Brdjanin was present there. I was at another such Crisis Staff meeting where I opposed -- and there was a lower-level police chief there, Tutus Vladimir. We opposed the establishment of a para-police which would control legality in the Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So when the question was asked how many ARK Crisis Staff meetings did you attend, you didn't mean the meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff; you meant the meetings of another Crisis Staff. Is that the explanation?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you continued to discuss the meeting that you attended, and now let's turn to page 16, you were asked the question at line 22: "At the meeting that you attended, were there any decisions made?" Answer: "I do remember, I opposed this," et cetera. And did Radoslav Brdjanin preside over this meeting? "He was there. I think he was chairing the meeting, but that's my recollection only." Again, your explanation is that you're referring not to the ARK Crisis Staff of which Mr. Brdjanin was president, but to another crisis staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just for the information of the Chamber, on page 16, we find some grey text as well. Is that the text that has not been immediately translated but is the result of later repeated listening to the original tape and then filling in the gaps left by the interpreter at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that's either filling in the gaps or providing an enhanced or clarified translation. But yes, the Court's understanding is accurate; that is part of the subsequent review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you've raised the -- you've raised Mr. Brdjanin's name and we've discussed Mr. Brdjanin's name in connection with the Crisis Staff. It's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Brdjanin publicly stated that only a certain percentage, a certain limited percentage of Muslims would be permitted to remain in the Banja Luka area; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned a percentage of 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's also correct that Mr. Brdjanin stated publicly, or reported publicly, on an incident during which he passed by the houses of Muslims and Croats who were making winter preparations, canning food and so on, and said to them words to the effect, "Do you really think you're going to spend the winter here?" And he stated that on TV; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brdjanin was thought of as the main civilian authority figure in the region; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he caused a great deal of satisfaction among the citizens, so many citizens came to see him, but I don't think that he could be considered the main authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, during your interview, you mentioned that people would come to speak with Brdjanin, provide him with all sorts of information about what was happening all over the area - and I'm referring now to page 22 - and you were asked if you thought that was because he was the president of the Crisis Staff, which people thought was the main authority in the region, and you said yes. Is that essentially correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to that, he made some kind of frustrating statements, and that was interesting, during the course of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no doubt that the remarks that we've just referred to and the hate-filled comments that Mr. Brdjanin directed toward Muslims and Croats enhanced his popularity, but my question is simple, and that is: Is it correct that you said that people came to him because he was the president of the Crisis Staff, which people thought of as the main civilian authority in the region, and that that answer was accurate?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know why they came to see him, because he was the president of the Crisis Staff or for some other reasons, but indeed they did come to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And indeed you did say during your interview that -- or you agreed during your interview that at least one of the reasons was because he was the president of the body that was seen as essentially the main authority in the region.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was considered the main authority, but the Assembly would either confirm or reject those decisions, the Assembly of the RK Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brdjanin was quite close to the republic leadership, and particularly to Mr. Karadzic, to Dr. Karadzic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of the ministers, for civil engineering and construction, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. But even before -- I mean, the fact that he became a minister after his tenure as president of the ARK Crisis Staff was a reflection of the close relationship he had with Dr. Karadzic and the republic leadership; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that all the MPs were equally close to Karadzic and all other leaders of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kasagic, you know that that is an inaccurate, to say the least, remark, if not logically impossible. But let me keep it simple. Didn't you say in your interview, very directly, that Mr. Brdjanin was close to Mr. Karadzic? And that's located at page 22. I'll repeat the question and answer for you if you need me to.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly I said that, but I'm not diminishing that in any way. I mean, I'm not saying that he's the only one who was close to him, but he was close to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This Court has had the benefit of seeing and hearing a number of telephone conversations between Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Karadzic. I'm not going to take you through those. There's one, for example, located in the binders that took place on October 31st. That's tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My mistake, Your Honour. It appears it's not listed as being in evidence yet, so I presume it needs a new number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. If the Court can give me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 6, Your Honours, will be P993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And while I won't take you through the whole intercept, at the bottom of page 3 of the English translation, and that would correspond to your B/C/S version as well, we see Dr. Karadzic frustrated by Mr. Brdjanin's constant contact with him and his constant request for instructions and direction, and saying: "Come on, man, finish that work. Don't call me for each petty thing. I'm not your nanny." And that was an accurate reflection of the regular contact between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Brdjanin and the reliance of Mr. Brdjanin on him, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about their telephone contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you were aware of their relationship, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew about it, as a member of parliament. Once Karadzic said, perhaps jokingly, that we would propose him minister for minority groups. Brdjanin, Karadzic, and I were present when he said that, but he never officially proposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was an amazingly cynical remark by Dr. Karadzic, wasn't it, proposing Radoslav Brdjanin as the minister of minorities.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But he never did it officially. He just said it once in the street, when we happened to meet up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the joke was that Dr. Karadzic knew full well Mr. Brdjanin's attitude and actions toward minorities; correct? That's the joke of that remark; right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I thought it was, because I never heard Radovan Karadzic mention it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the reliance by ARK officials on Dr. Karadzic and the republic leadership, reflected in the intercept we just looked at, continued on into the beginning of and throughout -- into the beginning of the war; let me just stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger, about this conversation, I'd like to remain in the same paragraph you've quoted: [In English] "Come on, man, finish that work. Don't call me for each petty thing. I am not your nanny." [Interpretation] I'm very interested in the following sentence, and I'd like to have the view of the witness on the following sentence, which reads as follows: [In English] "You have presidents of municipalities, exercise that power through them." [Interpretation] What does he mean here? And then the following sentence reads as follows: [In English] "Until we've established autonomy." [Interpretation] According to you, what does this sentence mean? [In English]: "You have the power in your hands, you have presidents of municipalities, exercise that power through them." [Interpretation] What did he mean by that? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was president of the Executive Council of municipalities, so I cannot come to any big conclusions, but I could have assumed that it had to do with the local authorities, not the republican authorities, and that the RK Krajina could handle these affairs at local level, not at republican level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make an observation, if I may, at this juncture? Immediately before Judge Hanoteau's question, Mr. Tieger said: "Now, the reliance by ARK officials on Dr. Karadzic and the republic leadership reflected in the intercept we just looked at continued," et cetera. Well, Your Honour, the witness hasn't looked at the intercept. I've made this type of objection before. The Court may be familiar with his intercept. It may previously have been adduced in evidence. The Court will have an opportunity to look at this intercept in due course. But if my learned friend is going to make an observation like that, then really the witness needs to deal with the whole of it; otherwise, I submit it's not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour. It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's some merit in what Mr. Josse says, that to confront the witness with your understanding of the whole of the transcript, which he could not review, and then ask questions, is perhaps not very helpful for the Chamber to make the determinations it will have to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in various ways, we all seem to be in agreement, so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The ARK leadership continued to turn to Dr. Karadzic for direction after October 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. I was not in the ARK leadership. I didn't work with them. I was too busy as president of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we've looked at the spoken words, albeit in writing, of one ARK leader. Let's turn now to a telephone intercept of another ARK leader in April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that can be found at tab 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P994, Your Honours, and English translation will be P994.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, P994 is a conversation between Vojislav Kupresanin and General Kukanjac in April of 1992. Mr. Kupresanin was the president of the ARK Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to a portion of the intercept found at the top of page 2 of the English translation, which I believe can be found at the top of page 3 of your translation, where Mr. Kupresanin says: "Well, we must and now we are waiting for Karadzic to return from Europe and tell us what we are to do next. I personally think, General, that I won't do anything until he returns, when he comes whatever he tells us we will do. He is now for us the supreme commander and we have no other commander. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the one side and the Serb people in the situation they are in, on the other. We have our commander, it is that man, we must obey him, you understand us, we understand you." Mr. Kasagic, is it your testimony that you were unaware of the relationship between the ARK leadership, including Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Brdjanin, and the republic leadership, and in particular, Dr. Karadzic? You didn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A special cooperation between the leadership and Karadzic, I didn't know about that. I know that individually, as members of parliament, they did cooperate with Karadzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you were -- your testimony is you were unaware of this hierarchical relationship. That's what you want to tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never understood the Krajina -- the ARK Krajina very seriously. The republican organs, that's different. I took that seriously. But in war, it was a renegade thing and they did their own things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I want to turn to a couple of other matters. During the course of your examination-in-chief by Mr. Josse, you were asked what you say to the suggestion that you, in conjunction with Mr. Zupljanin, became very wealthy from the illegal smuggling of fuel, and you gave a lengthy answer that included your comment that there were a lot of rumours in the war, that someone said you had a son with a company somewhere, although you don't have a son, that you didn't think Zupljanin was involved in the smuggling of oil, and especially with you, et cetera, et cetera. But I'm not sure that the thrust of the question was actually answered, and I just wanted some clarification on that. Were you saying that you were never involved in the business of oil or fuel with Mr. Zupljanin, or were you saying that whatever your involvement with oil and fuel did not result in any significant remuneration to you, or were you saying that you were never involved in oil and fuel in any way, shape, or form during that period; that is, the period 1991, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I was absolutely not involved in any way, nor was I interested in that. The Executive Council made it possible to supply oil to hospitals and schools, but that was the Executive Council, not Rajko Kasagic. I guarantee that 1.000 per cent, that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, just so I understand this correctly, because I don't want to have the same lack of clarity that prompted my question in the first place: Does that mean that the Executive Council was involved in some -- and that members of the Executive Council were involved in some way in supplying oil or fuel, but that you personally never got involved in it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I put it. The reserves of crude oil were obtained by the Executive Council with the Serb Krajina and the Ministry of Finance paid a company which made uniforms for the Serb Krajina in Croatia. And as president of the Executive Council, I had so much trouble --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. You were starting to get to the answer. I'm sorry to interrupt you. As president of the Executive Council ... Continue.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Council. The Executive Council. Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, maybe I can assist by -- in a further effort to narrow the question. It's pretty simple. I just wanted to find out if your answer was: Yes, the Executive Council got involved, but I, Rajko Kasagic, never got involved in any way, or you had something else in mind.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Executive Council participates in commodity reserves to this present day. That is one of its obligations. But, as an individual, no. Today it is the mayor who deals with these suppliers. It is no longer the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to distinguish between -- I want to find out your own physical efforts or lack of efforts. So does that mean you were involved in the transport, provision, smuggling, or anything else, of oil or fuel as a representative of the Executive Council, or that you were not involved in that in any way, shape, or form? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could we split that up in transport, provision, et cetera, and smuggling, which are, of course, two -- they can the same, but I'd like to hear from the witness first whether he performed any task in obtaining, transporting, et cetera. Would you please answer that question, whether you had any duty in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an individual, separately, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But ex officio, so from your position, you had to deal with obtaining reserves, getting it transported to the places where it was needed, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an individual, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said "ex officio." That means from your position. That is, if you are a member of the Executive Committee, that you, as a member of the Executive Committee, that you were involved in the Executive Committee arranging for obtaining, transporting, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the Executive Committee, without my presence because I was in Belgrade, decided to obtain 3.000 tonnes of crude oil. So that as an individual, it was not my duty ex officio to make that decision on my own; it was the collective organ that made that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did that happen only once that a decision was made to obtain large quantities of oil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crude oil on two occasions, and as for oil, those are small commodity reserves and it was the vice-president for the economy that was involved in that, not myself. It was his duty to look after commodity reserves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, second question: Did you ever learn about any irregularity in obtaining oil? Because Mr. Tieger asked you about smuggling. Smuggling, I take it, means that not the normal legal formalities are fulfilled, that it is -- did you ever learn about irregularities in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the municipal organ, nobody was ever said to participate in any irregular smuggling or procurement of oil. I don't know as for what went on in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether you ever learned about it. That's the first question. And then we might have some follow-up questions as to in what capacity you learned about it, as a private individual or as a -- I just want first to have my question answered whether you learnt about anything that could be considered or was considered by anyone to be irregular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lot of things are irregular in war. There was an economic blockade. And persons had to obtain oil in spite of this blockade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for an explanation why there was a need to choose irregular ways. My question simply is whether you learned, ever, about something that could be regarded as irregular in this respect. Whether there was any need for it might be my next question. If you'd like to add something to your answer, you'll be in a position to do that if you request to do so. I just want an answer to my question. Did you ever learn about irregularities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall hearing about any particular individual involved in irregularities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether there was any individual involved. I'm asking you whether you ever learned about irregularities. And we'll come to the details later. I'd like to have an answer to my question. It seems, as a matter of fact, that you are trying to circumvent my question by giving all kind of what you do not know and that you are more or less not inclined to answer. Did you ever learn about irregularities? Whether you knew about the persons who was involved, what the need was, what the reason was, I'm not interested at this moment. Did you ever learn about irregularities in the oil -- in obtaining the oil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to recall, not circumvent your question, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, "I can't recall hearing about any particular individual involved in irregularities," that answer implies, more or less, that you learned about irregularities, although not about the details, as far as particular individuals is concerned. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then tell us what you learned about irregularities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learnt that there was smuggling of oil and oil derivatives in boats across the river Drina. I learnt that oil was being brought to the river Drina in barrels loaded on donkeys and then transported to the Republika Srpska by boat, thus avoiding the blockade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. And may I ask you next time to answer right away my questions and not to drag it along for two or three or four minutes before you tell us. Give the answer to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, on two occasions the Executive Committee, in your absence, made certain decisions about obtaining oil, but that was the full extent of your involvement with the provision or transport of oil; is that basically it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't oil, it was mazut. Once I was absent and on the other occasion I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the full extent of your involvement, then, on the occasion when you were present, was it simply to be present when the Executive Committee made that decision or was there additional involvement in the provision of mazut?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a previous agreement about this with the authorities of the Serbian Krajina and then the Executive Committee was tasked with obtaining several thousand tonnes, and this was paid for and delivered. It was concerning Mazut.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I thought it was a simple question, but maybe it wasn't. It's basically this: Was the full extent of your involvement with the provision of mazut that you raised your hand and voted along with others, or however the decision was made, that such mazut should be provided?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was also present in the negotiations with the authorities of the Serbian Krajina in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you went to Croatia to negotiate the provision and supply of mazut to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They came to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And does that, therefore, encompass the full extent of your activities with respect to the provision of oil, or mazut?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all. In the other case, I was in Belgrade when the Executive Committee decided on procuring mazut without my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you were absent and then you came back and found out they'd made this decision in your absence; is that it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me on the phone to get my agreement, but we had no mobile phones at the time. So in my absence, they obtained it; in the meantime, there was a blockade. You couldn't pay the money back, and the mazut couldn't be delivered. So I managed to get the money transferred to a company in Backa Topola and we got flour for it instead of mazut.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right at the beginning. I think it was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I'd like to take a look now at a few intercepted telephone conversations, the first of which took place on November 13th, 1991, and that's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that will need a new exhibit number. I'm sorry, I was waiting for indication of the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P995, Your Honours, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, as you can see, this is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Radic, the president of the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly. And I want to direct your attention to a portion of that conversation which begins at the bottom of page 6. And that's when Mr. Radic begins talking about a problem with heating and the absence of mazut. Mr. Radic states: "... there will be no heating starting from Sunday ..." Dr. Karadzic says: "No heating what?" Radic says: "I do not have, do not have mazut." And Dr. Karadzic says: "Well, you will do that, mazut, through Mirko Krajisnik." Radic goes on to say: "I have reserves for two days ... And they took it to work on that one month ago, and they have not done it, they have not. "They got the money from the municipality, and they have not done anything." Dr. Karadzic says: "Why did they get the money, how did they get the money?" Then although it says Karadzic in the English, it's, I think, fairly clearly a response by Radic. He says: "Well, that's a question. Kasagic, Andjelko --" That's Mr. Grahovac, correct, that reference to Andjelko? "... that Mr. Savicic, they should explain where the money is, what happened with it, and thirty thousand billion, man." Then they continue. Dr. Karadzic provides a telephone number and says, at the top of page 8: "But Mirko is in Belgrade today. Krajisnik is in Belgrade today. ... Mirko Krajisnik, he will obtain everything for you, the distribution, and everything will go, the papers, through him, and everything." He goes on to say: "And we made it centralised, until this company, this, stock company is there, everything will go through this. So, they do not have any chance to gain some personal profit. And here there will be a profit of three dinars for our organs." Radic says: "Thank God." And Dr. Karadzic says: "And for the organs of the Party." Mr. Kasagic, that appears to reflect some connection with or involvement in the provision of mazut. What's Mr. Radic referring to? What was the money, and what was it for, and what happened with it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about 30 billion dinars. The Municipal Assembly approved this money for the heating plant, in order to obtain the fuel. The money was transferred to the account of the heating plant. The heating plant designated Zoran Savicic to obtain the mazut. The heating plant and the Municipal Assembly knew about this. He transferred the money to a Belgrade company. What was its name now? It was a big Serbian company. I can't recall the name now. But there was a blockade. Some of the mazut arrived, but most of the money was returned to the Municipal Assembly. Andjelko Grahovac knows full well that he threatened Savicic, telling him to send the money back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn next to an intercept dated November 18th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question. You said, "There was a blockade. Some of the mazut arrived." How did that arrive, despite the blockade? Could you tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It arrived from the Serb Krajina. How they managed to get it, I don't know. Radovan Bajic, as the vice-president of the Executive Committee, would know that better than me. Although there was a blockade, there was also a de-blockade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether finally it was legally transported and delivered or whether there was any circumventing a blockade involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was legally obtained from the Serbian Krajina, because there was no blockade between the Serbian Krajina and the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before I turn to the next intercept, I wanted to ask you a couple of additional questions about this one. We see Dr. Karadzic directing Mr. Radic to Mirko Krajisnik. Was Mirko Krajisnik associated with any company involved in or connected with the provision of oil or fuel?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what the Boksit company was?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boksit Milic? It was in Milici. Rajko Dukic was the director of that company. It was a state-owned company, a big company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Rajko Dukic is also the president of the SDS Executive Committee; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did hold a post. I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Rajko Dukic or Boksit involved in the provision of mazut, or oil, or fuel?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that. It was far away from Banja Luka municipality. It's near the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is not whether you can. Distance as such does not prevent you from having any knowledge. Do I have to understand your answer to be that you have no knowledge? Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to an intercept located at tab 43, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, P996 is a conversation in January 1992 between Rajko Dukic and Momcilo Krajisnik. As you can see at the beginning of the conversation, Mr. Dukic says: "Good morning." Mr. Krajisnik says: "Hey, hello Rajko." And Mr. Dukic says: "I have had some conversations, won't talk about it over the phone, but here with me is Kasagic and we're trying to do some other things, but here's what I'm calling about." And if we turn to page 2 of the English translation, and also page 2 of the B/C/S version before you, we can see that Mr. Krajisnik says: "Let's go to the club. Where are you now?" Mr. Dukic says: "We are here, and Kasagic is with me, looking for mazut, fuck it. Banja Luka is freezing cold. No mazut." Mr. Krajisnik says: "Okay. Check it out and we'll meet later." Mr. Dukic says: "And Mirko is not here, so I took over his jobs. I'm doing something." Mr. Krajisnik says: "Good, okay." Mr. Dukic says: "Here, still think over that variant." Mr. Krajisnik says: "Okay, fine." And they say goodbye. Is this another incident that your memory has failed you on, Mr. Kasagic, meeting personally with Mr. Dukic in pursuit of mazut? Mr. Dukic, the man about whom you said you had no idea whether he had any involvement in the provision of such commodities?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't remember this. When I was at Pale, I was with many people, including Dukic. I don't recall discussing it with him. But mazut was indispensable for the hospital. I don't even know that we procured it through Dukic. As far as I can recall, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So mazut was indispensable. You went out in pursuit of it, met with Mr. Dukic, at least on this occasion, if not others, to get it, and yet this pursuit of this indispensable commodity has somehow completely escaped your recollection, or at least that's what you want the Court to believe; is that it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't, because these were all jobs for the republican government, not for the Executive Committee. However, I was out on the ground and I knew what the problems were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And according to you, obtaining oil was indispensable, and yet you have assured the Court 1.000 per cent that you never had any personal involvement in it. That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not financially, but in discussions, there were discussions. But I came out with an empty pocket in 1996, and I had to enrol in a Ph.D. course in order to get financial assistance, because I had empty pockets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, it takes us quite some time to get from one point, where you said once oil -- I think you were talking about crude oil -- was ordered when I was not there; and once I was present when the person in charge of economics said that we had to decide on that, he decided; and I had no further involvement whatsoever. After half an hour, the story is quite different. Why didn't you say right from the beginning: Of course I was involved in trying to find that oil and mazut, because it was of major importance for the hospital, but whoever gained any money out of that, not me personally, although I was really involved in trying to get it. Why didn't you say that at the beginning? Why does it take us half an hour? Why does it take me ten minutes to get you to -- that you knew about smuggling? I'm not saying that you were involved. I just wanted to learn whether you ever heard about it. Why don't you say directly these kind of things? It's not wrong to seek oil for a hospital, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's only that additional questions additionally jog my memory. I don't really remember this with Dukic now. I know where funds were involved, and where they were not, I cannot recall exactly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think I jogged your memory on the smuggling issue. I didn't know anything about it. I couldn't give you any information about it. It was only by asking five times the same question that you clearly did not answer. And when your answers clearly indicated that you knew more but you are not very much inclined to tell, and only confronted with that attitude, you finally came up with barrels of oil going over a river. I'm not blaming anyone for, but we just want to have the information. So you're now instructed to answer questions as they are put to you, and not only to tell the truth that you find most relevant, but the whole truth in relation to the question put to you, and not after the fifth question, but immediately after the first question. We'll adjourn until five minutes -- until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I deal with one matter in the absence of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll adjourn, but Mr. Josse wanted to address us on a matter unknown to us yet. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I concede that the witness was not answering all the questions directly, but whether what Your Honour just said to the witness was entirely fair is perhaps a moot point. I mean, earlier on, he made it clear that he wasn't a thousand per cent involved. He then went on to -- he was then asked another question by Mr. Tieger, which ended: "But you personally never got involved with it?" And then he said, "That's not the way I put it." And then he began to explain the reserves of crude oil were obtained by the Executive Council, and then we came to the point where Mr. Tieger interrupted him. Now, I've already conceded, Your Honour - and I'm deliberately not doing this in the presence of the witness - that he wasn't giving, on occasions, direct answers to the questions that were being put to him. But in my submission, what Your Honour has just said to him doesn't accurately reflect 100 per cent the question and answers at that particular juncture of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly -- what exactly do you have in mind? Because I take it serious, Mr. Josse, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: About page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what I said which was unfair, the exact point, because then I'll ... I asked him why he did not give -- I said that it took us quite some time to get from the one point that he said there was only -- I wasn't there. People took positions and then ... What's the unfair -- where did I say something, and what exactly? I take it that you're referring to pages 30 and 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I take it seriously. If I would unfairly treat the witness, I would correct that. But tell me exactly where -- what line I spoke was unfair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Particularly the words: "And I had no further involvement whatsoever."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't that how it started in the beginning? Didn't he say, "Well, the only thing I know is that once they ordered 300 tonnes, I think, in --" I only pointed at how it started. I didn't say that during that half an hour, we did not slowly get to the new situation. I depicted there the situation as we perceived it, on the basis of the answers to the first questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I put it like this: That it's quite clear from the demeanour and tenor of the witness's evidence from the outset that he's at great pains to say that he didn't profit personally from any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He also made it clear, albeit in a painful way, I concede, that he had some knowledge of his municipality being involved in the attaining of fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to persist with the point, Your Honour. And I'm not asking Your Honour to say anything more to him, because I do accept that the witness needed some cajoling in relation to answering these questions in a direct manner. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'll review it carefully and my -- I'll endeavour that what I say to a witness is not for 95 or 98 true but for the full hundred per cent. That's what I'm aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one brief observation, and that is that I think Mr. Josse was inadvertently inaccurate when he recounted the witness's testimony as being that he wasn't involved a thousand per cent. It's a little bit different, which was he said he wasn't involved in any way, and he guaranteed that 1.000 per cent. It's a slight difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't want to comment on that, because I noticed it as well. Let's -- I think we could all agree that the cross-examination of the witness might be more fruitful if direct answers were given to the questions put to him. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed, but I'd first inform the parties that, where I said yesterday that I would inform one waiting witness not later than 11.00, that he doesn't have to remain standby this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I helpfully received that message and have asked one of our staff to pass the message on to VWS. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, returning briefly to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The Court has previously received in evidence an order dated May 4th, 1992, from the Autonomous Region of Krajina, that was issued pursuant to the decision of the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That republic-level decision was issued 16 April 1992. It's correct that the Autonomous Region of Krajina received and implemented orders and directives from the republic level during 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but that probably was the case, because they cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may, let me turn your attention to two additional exhibits located at tabs 24 and 43, I believe. Correction, that's 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 24 needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And 44 would need --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P998, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at those quickly, Mr. Kasagic. First, P997 is a public announcement dated 6 June 1992, signed by the president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Vojo Kupresanin, which states that: "On behalf of the Serbian people of the Krajina, the Presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina hereby renounces the legitimacy of Nenad Kecmanovic and Mirko Pejanovic to represent the Serbian people in any capacity." It goes on to say: "The Serbian people is proud of its heroes to the same extent that it detests traitors and degenerates such as the two mentioned." And then it disassociates itself from them. And then if you could look quickly at tab 44, you'll see contained there a telegram log of telegrams transmitted between April and November 1992. And if we look at page 4 of the English translation, at the bottom, and page -- the page designated 00583895 at the top of the B/C/S translation, you'll see an entry for a telegram sent on 5 June 1992 at 1210 hours. The summary is: "Disassociation from the participation of Pejanovic and Kecmanovic in the BH Presidency." The sender is the government. And among the recipients is the autonomous district or region in Banja Luka. That's another reflection of an order or directive sent by the republic level to the Autonomous Region of Krajina that was implemented; correct, Mr. Kasagic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this, but I know that we did not hear about the work of these two in the Presidency in that period at all; whether they were doing something, whether they were making any decisions, we had no idea. I really had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's in part the point, that although you didn't know about it in Krajina, the government in Pale did and so they issued this instruction via telegram and it was implemented by Mr. Kupresanin; right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me move on, then, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it's not entirely clear to me, because in your question you interpret more or less this tab 44 by saying that this is another example of an order or directive, where from what I see at this moment, it could, well, be information -- because I do understand that it has to do with the functioning of two persons in the BH Presidency, which I would be inclined to understand as something that happened on the highest level and of which the lower levels were informed, rather than -- I have some difficulties in understanding how this should be implemented on the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I appreciate the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's another example of the republic level providing information about a position to be taken to the regions which was acted upon or followed up on by the regions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, perhaps if you would have an additional mouse pad to put under the microphone, because I don't want Ms. Javier to type and at the same time I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Give us a moment and we'll see if we have -- I think the problem has been resolved by the usher, but maybe we can address that a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I wanted next to address with you an issue that was raised during the course of your direct examination, and that's the question of what you knew or heard about crimes committed against the Muslim and Croat population in 1992.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Banja Luka or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question that was raised was what you knew as a general matter. In fact, the question was: "Were you aware of any discussion --" among the questions asked in connection with that issue was: "Were you aware of any discussion, informally, amongst deputies, about crimes that were being committed in Bosnia?" And you said: "Publicly, at the Assembly session, no such thing was discussed. However, from the Prijedor deputies, I learnt that there was a public camp in Prijedor - Keraterm, I believe it was called - and that was the information I had." First of all, Mr. Kasagic, what did you learn about the Keraterm camp in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that it was mostly Muslims who were in their camp, and I know that one man from Banja Luka happened to be in that camp, and when he was freed, he came back. His brother was my neighbour. What happened there exactly is something I don't know, because I was never in that camp myself. I heard that there were about 7.000 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I take it from your answer, although I guess you can clarify it if I'm mistaken, that because you were asked about crimes committed in Bosnia and responded, in part, about Keraterm, that you learned something to the effect that crimes were committed against the Muslim detainees in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear anything beyond that, what happened to them, but I also heard that there were some camps, a few camps, in Sarajevo. What happened to the prisoners is something I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I actually don't recall asking about Sarajevo, so I'll ask you to concentrate on the area we're discussing. Did you receive any information informally to the effect that the detainees in Keraterm were civilians, to the effect that the conditions in Keraterm were inhumane or brutal, or that crimes had been committed in connection with the operation of the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they were civilians. Which crimes were committed, I don't know, but I heard that some people were killed. How many were killed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you hear that from deputies from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Srdjo talked about that, Srdjan. I forgot his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was Keraterm the only detention facility that you heard anything about during 1992 from your fellow deputies or from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Keraterm from the media. Now, was it somewhere else too, I don't know, but I can't remember. Keraterm was often mentioned, so that's how I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, the question was a little bit different. It was whether or not Keraterm was the only detention facility about which you've heard. You've already told us you heard about Keraterm, and in fact you already told us you heard it informally from the Prijedor deputies. Now I want to know if you heard about other detention facilities from anyone else during 1992.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could we, just to avoid whatever understanding ... When Mr. Tieger asks you about detention facilities, would you please include in your answer centres, camps, whatever name it had, but where you received information that a larger number of peoples were together, not in their own homes, but gathered at a certain place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's only Prijedor that I heard of, as far as a large group of people are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Smaller groups you heard about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was mention that there were some individuals in the camp of Manjaca, in Banja Luka. That was a military camp. How many people were there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No other -- that's in Banja Luka. That's not in Prijedor. No other centres - well, whatever name; camps, facilities - in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's true for the whole of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I may return to the question of your informal discussions with your fellow deputies or other representatives of Republika Srpska, but first I wanted to turn to your remark during your direct examination that publicly at the Assembly sessions no such thing was discussed, meaning no -- there was no discussion about crimes that were being committed in Bosnia. I'm referring to page 74 of the LiveNote of your direct examination. Mr. Kasagic, you may or may not be aware of the fact that this Court has had an opportunity to receive and review transcripts of many of the Assembly sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly from 1991 and 1992 and onward, and is therefore familiar with a great many things that were said during the course of the Assembly sessions. I want to draw your attention to some of those, to see if that somehow jogs your memory about the kinds of things that were discussed, the kinds of issues that were raised at the Assembly sessions in 1992. And just as a few examples, on May 12th, 1992, the minister of health, Dragan Kalinic, spoke about how perfidious the enemy is, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily, destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people. He also spoke about the military hospital in Sarajevo and told the Assembly that he was for the destruction of the hospital so that the enemy has nowhere to go for medical help. At the same session, Mr. Vjestica talked about the fact that on the right bank of the Una River there were no more Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, that they had been evacuated, and asked rhetorically: "Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely, after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border." Mr. Radic, on that -- at that same session, spoke about shelling and destroying towns, and referred to the destruction of one third of the town. At the 17th Session, in July of 1992, a delegate spoke about his reaction to hearing -- to a visit by Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik in Ilidza and how the Bosnian Serbs were able to extend their territory, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been a majority. At the same session, Mr. Dukic, to whom we had occasion to refer earlier, talked about having expelled all Muslim judges from Vlasenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik, talked about the situation in Birac, which had 120.000 Muslims, but he hoped that had been at least halved. At the same session, Mr. Nedic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm not -- you gave quite a lot of examples. I can imagine that you would find a few more, but perhaps we could ask the witness, unless you think that the complete quotations are --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two more, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two more. Yes. Make it quick, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, in the July session, Mr. Milanovic spoke about the problem of captured persons and spoke about hundreds and thousands of prisoners. And Mr. Nedic and Mr. Karadzic spoke about the Muslims having been planted to the Serbs as a people whose executioners they were to be, or that the conflict was roused in order to eliminate Muslims. Now, as the Court indicated, I could continue for quite some time, but I want to ask you now, Mr. Kasagic, having heard just a sampling of those references, if that refreshes your recollection that the subject of crimes against Muslims and Croats was publicly discussed, or at least openly discussed, at Assembly sessions, some of which may have been closed, among the delegates, and that you were, therefore, aware of that.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not wish to hide anything, but I really do not remember that. I'd really like to say everything, to the extent to which I was involved, but it has been 13 years, and I cannot remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, let me make it clear that I am not asking you to recall in precise detail the comments of each deputy or the specific information imparted. What I'm asking you is: During the course of your attendance at these Assembly sessions - and you told us you considered it an obligation to attend every Assembly session - isn't it true that, as a general matter, you learned that Muslims and Croats were being forcibly expelled from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as a legalist, didn't you make an effort to talk to your fellow deputies to see how that could be stopped? You didn't do that, did you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't any good. In Nova Gradiska, it was asked why there were Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka, and I went out and I said: You who live in villages don't know what it's like to live in a city. There is 58.000 Muslims and Croats. The international community would not allow that kind of attitude towards these people. It would be a column from Banja Luka all the way up to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kasagic, again, this is not an answer to the question. I do understand that you want to draw our attention to the fact that perhaps in Banja Luka things went differently and that there was no way that you would drive out 58.000 people. But the question was a totally different one. The question was: When you heard in the Assembly about forcible expulsion, not from Banja Luka but that that happened, the question was whether you did talk to your fellow deputies to see how that could be stopped. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I did not talk to them and that Marinko Kontic, one deputy, said before the war started: We will have to see how we're going to live with these people, and it is our destiny to live with these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us that you heard that Muslims had been expelled by force. That's what you've said. For you, did it imply that there were detention camps set up where these people were sent after they were expelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know of camps in Prijedor, but I haven't heard of any others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of any camps. If they were expelled, it doesn't mean that they were detained in camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kasagic, since you learned about this at the sessions of the Assembly, you weren't the only one who knew about this; all the representatives of the Serbian Republic knew about this, didn't they, knew about the forcible expulsion of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to a different -- slightly different issue at the moment, and I want to turn my attention next to -- strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to turn my attention next to two issues that you raised. The first is the question you were asked during the course of your examination about a document that was referred to as the Variant A and B document, which you indicated you saw for the first time in The Hague, and said that you didn't remember hearing of it in 1992, and if you did, you forgot. Now --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Kasagic, do you think it's possible if I directed your attention to some occasions on which you heard references to Variant A and B before coming to The Hague, that it might jog your memory about whether or not you ever heard of this document?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe when I hear you jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the 6th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, on January 26th, 1992, Mr. Cizmovic spoke. Were you present at that session? And he spoke about some issues related to what the Serbian -- the Bosnian Serb authorities needed to do next. And he said: "To solve this problem, I propose that we begin with an urgent operationalisation and a declaration on the establishment and promulgation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and Herzegovina. Tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out."

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was in Holiday Inn, I remember that Assembly session. That's when the Council of Ministers was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you remember now Mr. Cizmovic making a direct and explicit reference to the 19 December 1991 instructions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't recall any individual contributions to the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall now that by at least that time, you were aware of the existence of the Variant A and B document, the 19 December 1991 instructions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not of significance in actual life, so I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
