utterances.text: Well, that's a pretty sweeping statement, Mr. Kasagic, for the president of the Executive Committee in Banja Luka. Or were you aware of the extent to which the Variant A and B document was received and recorded and reflected in the minutes of municipalities all over the Serbian Republic? Do you have that information? Are you able to tell the Court that you know the extent to which, if at all, other municipalities received and recorded this document?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I've already referred you to what happened in January 26th, when Mr. Cizmovic said: "The tasks set out in the instructions of 19 December 1991 should be carried out." Let me turn your attention next to an extended session of the SDS Main and Executive Boards on 14 February 1992, during which Dr. Karadzic spoke. Do you recall being present at that session?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the SDS organs at republic level, I didn't attend, because I was not a member of the Executive Board of the SDS at republican level but, rather, at the level of Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, the question was about the Main and Executive Boards. You said you were not a member of the Executive Board. Were you not a member of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was a member of the Executive Board of Banja Luka municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the session, Mr. Kasagic, Mr. Dukic indicates that among those invited were the presidents of municipal executive committees. Does that jog your recollection about whether or not you attended this session?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I certainly never attended a single session of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that something else you guarantee 1.000 per cent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't guarantee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, let me show you the next exhibit. It's found at tab 45. As you can see, Mr. Kasagic, this is a receipt from the Holiday Inn for February 14th and 15th, 1992, indicating that you stayed there. Name: Kasagic, SDS Assembly, paid by SDS. So in view of the fact that you were in Sarajevo on that date, staying at the Holiday Inn, where this meeting was held, and had been invited ex officio to this meeting, does that now jog your recollection about your presence?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that I was at the Assembly held in the Holiday Inn of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. It's possible I may have been there too, but I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to turn your attention to some of the references during the course of that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if the witness could have the B/C/S in front of him. This is a transcript of remarks at the February 14th session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's tab --?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 13. And for the record, Your Honour, that's P67, intercept tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, you indicated that you had --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A question arises in respect of the Holiday Inn bill and receipt. It said that it's 64A, but that's, as far as I understand, footnotes to the Treanor binder. So I don't think, then, that the actual documents are in evidence. So that's footnote material. Yes, okay. Then that's clear. Please proceed. I apologise. We're at tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I think you indicated that you had a chance to look at the Variant A and B document, that Mr. Josse or someone else showed it to you when you arrived in The Hague, so I take it, therefore, you could see that it was broken down into two variants, hence its name, Variant A and B, and into two stages or levels for the stages of implementation. Let me now turn your attention to four separate references to stage 2. First, at page 5 and 6 of the English translation. Dr. Karadzic says: "But also, that a bird cannot come in without your, without your knowledge. That is, if you remember, who keeps that in mind, or maybe not on his person, a stage number 2. There is, remember, you know what I am talking about? - We know. Yes. That is, therefore, the stage number 2, the second stage in smaller or bigger variations, but you have to implement that slowly now, to have absolute control who is travelling along your roads, what are they transporting --"

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The witness hasn't got the place, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just try to assist the witness in finding the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's found at 04002200, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kasagic, you would see that on the top of the page, last four digits, 2200.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, on the very next page, again approximately in the middle of the page, Dr. Karadzic says, during the course of a reference to the BiH government referendum: "The second thing that is very important, it gives us full moral right not to accept any decision resulting from the referendum and it gives us right to introduce the stage number 2 in functioning of your area ..." The next reference I want to turn your attention to during the course of Dr. Karadzic's speech is found at page 17 of the English translation and page 2208 of your version, toward the bottom of the page. Again, another reference to stage number 2. Dr. Karadzic says: "The stage number 2 should also be converted, the one we've talked about, the one you have if not here, at home." And finally, on page 24 of the English translation, and page 2214 of your version, at the top of the page, Dr. Karadzic says: "That is why we called you today, to intensify, to introduce the second level and to intensify the functioning of the government at any cost and on every single millimetre of our territory." And finally, Mr. Kasagic, lest there be any lingering question about your attendance at that session, let me just direct your attention quickly to page 26 of the English translation and page 2215 of your version, where there's a reference to what you and Mr. Kupresanin had said. Mr. Kasagic, do you now recall, having looked at the multiple references at a meeting which, as Dr. Karadzic indicated, was called to intensify and to introduce the second level, do you now recall that you were aware of the 19 December 1991 instructions, a Variant A and B document, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that I was present, according to this, but whether it was the Assembly or the party, I don't know. I know I was in the Holiday Inn. I don't know the date. And I recall my contribution to the discussion, if that's the date, but I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, that was not the question. At least, the -- the question was whether you now recall that you were aware of the 19 December 1991 instructions, a Variant A and B document. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Really, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just directly now ask you: It seems that a first stage and a second-stage issue appears prominently during this meeting. So I'm not talking about 19th of December and what's Variant A, Variant B. Do you remember that there was such a thing as something to be developed in two stages, which seems to prominently appear in the record of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection on being at this meeting, not understanding at all what Mr. Karadzic was talking about, about these two stages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attended a meeting at the Holiday Inn. Whether it was this meeting or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, two minutes ago you said it appears that it was on that meeting, on the basis of the record, and you have been confronted with the, well, hotel bills of that same day. So now, were you at that meeting or were you not at that meeting? Or is it that you say: Well, I have to conclude on the basis of these papers that I have been at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can conclude on the basis of these papers that I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, again my question, which was: Do you have any recollection of being at a meeting where Mr. Karadzic even explained why that meeting was called, that is, to -- second stage to be implemented, to be started, and you sitting there having no clue about what he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember at the meeting you attended that Mr. Karadzic did give a speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We all spoke. How much he spoke and what he said, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, there continued to be references to the Variant A and B document, to the instructions of 19 December 1991, after 1992. And let me give you two examples of that at Assembly sessions where you were present. First, at the 46th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, held on the 9th through the 11th and the 23rd of November, 1994, where Dr. Karadzic was talking about the instructions A and B and clearly making references to how important they were. He said: "Please remember what it was like before the war. Everything was perfectly clear to us in those municipalities where we were in the majority and in those where we were in the minority. You remember instructions A and instructions B? We had crisis staffs which clearly knew that they were in power there. They might have made mistakes, but they were the authorities."

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall any individual items on the agenda. I'm not trying to conceal anything; I simply don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember that at any of these later Assembly meetings any reference was made to something like A and B or first and second stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall A and B. I only recall the goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not -- yes. And what were the goals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that Karadzic propounded the goals, more at the initiative of the army, which said they didn't know what they were fighting for, and he said it was for the demarcation between the other two communities, that the internal borders had not been properly established, and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been recognised. There was mention of Sarajevo and the division of Sarajevo. I understood this all to be part of the work of the Badinter Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me pursue that a bit. You're not suggesting that it was the Badinter Commission representatives who decided that Bosnia should be ethnically divided and who decided that the borders for Republika Srpska should be the Una, the Neretva, and the Sava, and the Drina?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the Lisbon Agreement, in fact. I misspoke. As far as I can recall, it was not Badinter. His name was something else. He was the president, or rather, the Prime Minister of Portugal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. You're talking about Mr. Cutileiro; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Cutileiro. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let's be clear on what you're saying. Are you suggesting that the goals, the strategic goals of Republika Srpska, were formulated by Mr. Cutileiro and that he decided that Bosnia should be ethnically divided? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't dividing us from each other, but there was division into regions. This was before the war and the representatives of all three parties agreed to it; Izetbegovic and I think Karadzic for the Serbs, and Kljuic, in Lisbon. It was signed in Lisbon, but however, when the party representatives returned to Sarajevo, Mr. Izetbegovic went back on the agreement. It had to do with the regionalisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So there was no agreement. And then the Bosnian Serb authorities began to implement, through their military forces, the goals of ethnically dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina and the goals of demarcating the territory?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Demarcating the territory, yes, but I did not understand it to be ethnic demarcation, because no one forbade anyone to live in other territories though belonging to a different group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It included claiming and attempting to gain control over territories on which the Bosnian Serbs were a minority because, according to the Bosnian Serb authorities, of the genocide of World War II; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Genocide in the Second World War was mentioned, but to what extent control, or gaining control, was talked about, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The territory of Republika Srpska was meant to include, according to the goals that you mentioned, and according to the constitution, land on which the Serbs were a minority and the Muslims were a majority, and the reason given was because of the genocide of World War II; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You never heard of that, that provision in the constitution or that general goal to ensure that territory on which the Serbs were a minority because of World War II became part of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mentioned, and Article 1 of the constitution said that Republika Srpska is the state of the Serbian people and that there was sovereignty involved, but the international community did not recognise that, so all of it was abolished altogether. So elements of statehood were abolished, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, because that's not a direct answer to the question: Were you aware that territories where the Serbs were a minority were claimed to be a part of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that in all the municipalities which were considered by the Republika Srpska to be within its territory, that in all these municipalities before the war, the Serbs were in a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. In some, they were even a minority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when I said: "Were you aware that territories where the Serbs were a minority were claimed to be part of Republika Srpska," the answer is that for some of the municipalities that would be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seemed to be that way, in the case of some municipalities, because closer to Belgrade, in the area of Posavina, some municipalities had a Muslim or a Croat majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It didn't seem to be that way; it was that way, wasn't it? Yes. I see you're nodding yes. That's on the record now. Mr. Tieger, please proceed. Perhaps I add one thing, Mr. Kasagic. There's no need -- Mr. Kasagic -- please, if you could look in my direction, Mr. Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, there's no need to take a defensive attitude. We'd just like to know what you know and what you experienced, and just to tell us. If you take a defensive approach, to the extent that you are thinking about what you find most relevant to tell us, then we might miss useful information which could be in favour of either party. As a legalist, please make it possible for us, as Judges, to give the right decision at the end of this trial, and by being open and frank, we might better understand what it was all about and to better be capable of giving of right decisions. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kasagic, you clarified to some extent, after initially denying that territories on which Serbs were a minority, allegedly because of the genocide of World War II, was claimed by Republika Srpska, but in fact you've been well aware of that for a long time and publicly made that assertion; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a written record of that, then yes, I know that Serbs were a majority in Bihac, but they became a minority. But in Posavina, I believe the situation was different vis-a-vis the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kasagic, let me put it this way: During your examination-in-chief, you referred to yourself, I think more than once, as a legalist, drew attention to humanitarian gestures on your part, and indicated that you joined the SDS only because you wanted to fight communism, I think you said. That doesn't really tell the whole story, does it, Mr. Kasagic? In fact, you were somebody who was proud of the SDS programme and who, among other things, proudly proclaimed the goal of recovering territory on which Serbs had been subjected to genocide, resulting in the expulsion, the forcible expulsion, of the Muslim population from those parts; isn't that right? I'm not saying you believe it now, but you believed it then and said it then.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After these territories were taken, Serbs primarily stayed and Muslims and Croats moved out. That's as far as Posavina was concerned. What I said, I don't remember, but that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were among those people during the course of the war who spoke about the Muslims and Croats as enemies, who talked about the genocide perpetrated in World War II, the need to have that territory for Republika Srpska, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that I said that, but I don't remember all the things that I said. It's possible that I said it, but I never believed that other people should be expelled from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you were present at the Assembly sessions and the gatherings where Dr. Karadzic said that you couldn't live with Muslims, and spoke about the demographic threat presented by the Muslims, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that meant, as Brdjanin said, that the Muslim population had to be reduced to a certain percentage, so that Republika Srpska could be secure, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's roughly the way it was, yes. The figure of 5 per cent was bandied about, where national minorities would not threaten the majority nation. That's the same thing that was being said in Croatia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one additional question. You said -- the question was that 5 per cent, or lower, would be a situation in which there was no threat to a majority any more, and you said, when you were asked if Mr. Brdjanin said that the Muslim population had to be reduced, so that Republika Srpska could be secure ... In most of the municipalities, the Muslim part of the population was, even if it was a minority, was still well above 5 per cent. How did you then understand this to take place, reduction below 5 per cent? Do I have to understand this in relation to what you earlier testified, that forcible expulsion was what took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Banja Luka had 14.8 Muslims and 14.9 per cent Croats, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking just about Banja Luka. When you said when you understood that there was forcible expulsion, you remember talking about an Assembly meeting, and that was not just Banja Luka. I'm talking about the area of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the figure of 5 per cent is being mentioned, then the surplus, so to speak, has to be moved out, and also the economy was on the decline. Only 10 per cent of the economy of Banja Luka was functioning, so there was no employment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you understood, when you said that you learned in the Assembly that there was forcible expulsion, you understood this to be that part of the population had to be moved out in order to reduce it under 5 per cent -- part of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never understood it that way, that only 5 per cent would remain of other ethnic groups on that territory, or on any territory. I thought that everybody would go back after the war. Today, in the twenty-first century, that is impossible to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but as long as the war lasted, they, as you said, that the surplus above 5 per cent had to be moved out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Armed people were expelling them from their apartments, but there were no decisions that they had to be expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but it was the factual situation, and did you understand this in the context of reducing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the number of the Muslim population, the percentage of Muslim population below what was acceptable for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that it was temporary, a temporary move, but it is certain that some people will never come back to Banja Luka, including Serbs. They stayed abroad. Their children don't want to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you have been confronted, and this Chamber has received some evidence of public statements or non-public conversations in which it was said that one could not live together with the Muslims. How should the Chamber understand your testimony, saying that this was just temporary, in view of such statements that one could not live together with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I, as a lawyer, know about the universal declaration of human rights, that private property cannot be seized, and that everybody has the right to return to their own private property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what about the forcible expulsion of citizens of a certain ethnicity? Falls that within the scope of the universal declaration of human rights, even if it's temporary, well, let's say for a couple of years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't fit into it at all. It is a bare minimum, as far as the universal declaration is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that although the forcible removal took place, that it was not on the basis of a decision, that, as far as I understand you, it just happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that was my understanding too, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also told us that you learned in the Assembly, in the Republican Assembly, about forcible expulsion of Muslims, that you understood that that was the case. Do you remember any decision or any initiative within the Assembly saying: People are forcibly expelled? That's without any decision, so we should now take a decision that it should immediately start to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not only that I heard about it in the Assembly, but I also saw it in Gornji Vakuf, for example. I saw that civilians were being expelled by soldiers to the Federation. At the Assembly, I do not remember that there were decisions to put that to a stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you learned about such forcible expulsion in the Assembly, you saw it with your own eyes, and that, nevertheless, no effective initiatives were taken to put an end to it; is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood that right, but it was only peace that could have brought that to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. Oh, I'm looking at the clock. We are at a time to have a break, but I do not know whether -- I shouldn't ask you whether it's a suitable moment, because I interrupted your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us any estimate on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll certainly consume the rest of the day. During the recess I'll do my best to -- well, I'm frankly not optimistic about completing, but I'll try to move as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If perhaps Madam Usher could escort the witness out of the courtroom, and we'll have a break for some 20 minutes, Mr. Kasagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, at a certain moment I wondered what the use was of putting again to the witness what on paper he had attended and where he had no recollection of many, many things that were said there. And perhaps I added to it as well, but there comes a moment when the impression of the testimony takes its form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate the guidance, Your Honour, and I'll try to proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's at least one procedural matter that I need to mention today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it about scheduling in the near future?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start, but it had to do something with what you requested, Mr. Josse. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I indicated before the recess that I wanted to move to the next exhibit, which is a videotape of a mass rally that took place on 21 August 1994. It's found at tab 32, and was previously admitted as P357. Mr. Kasagic, I'll mention to you, as the Court is already aware, that this is a rally at which, among others, Mr. Brdjanin spoke, saying, among other things, "It was the obligation of Serbs over the next hundred years to wipe their feet from the foul non-Christians who had befouled this soil of ours." And at the end of the rally Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic speak, but you were also a speaker at that rally and I'd like, in connection with some of the earlier comments you made, I'd like to play your remarks on that occasion now. For the benefit of the interpreters, those can be found at 00:39:11. At least, that's where they begin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Brothers and sisters, God be with you! The people who are with God - God is with them! Those people cannot lose. Not from the most difficult edicts they are sending us from the West ... the same edicts which after the Berlin Congress expelled the Turkish ... trousers from these areas and introduced Viennese bureaucratese. Today they want to achieve the opposite. But we know all the evil with which they threaten us. They cannot deceive us again. We forgave, we forgot and that's why we are repeating our history. We no longer have the right to do that, because of our children, because of our grandfathers, because of our own selves. They offer us peace, but that peace, according to them, turns out to be a Muslim Islamic republic. They want that republic on our lands, with their army leader, a Bosnian army general tells the army: 'Your state stretches as far as your boot does.' And why should we behave differently? We have our state, we are defending it, we have established our borders and we shall defend them. They tell us - we do not recognise genocide, genocide. That is inscribed in our constitution. Our lands are in all those areas and territories where they perpetrated genocide against our people. Accordingly, we understand each other extremely well. But those under the Vatican's influence do not understand us. But we have agreed and we only have to achieve and sign that peace in which the Serbs will be equal and that the Serbs will never accept tutelage. It seems they don't understand us ... but we're not asking them to understand us. That is why they are trying us in their courts, that is why they are burning our truth, but that fire will not burn because of our truth, nor will our truth burn in that fire. Those judges of theirs cannot talk with us. They don't know how, they don't have the facts on their side. We have joined the land and the sky, so no earthly power, not even NATO's aircraft, can do anything to us. They think ... they think we have stumbled, allegedly the Serbs have quarrelled, but they forget or perhaps don't know, from their student who wrote Jablan, a Viennese student, that the bull only wins after it stumbles. We have won and have established our border. "Brothers and sisters, I listened to the news today, they are coming from France and offering a half-baked peace to our brothers in Serbia ... in Serbia. They said they would gradually lift sanctions only in the sphere of culture and sports and the airport in Belgrade, only on condition that NATO forces, or rather their forces come to the banks of the Drina. Accordingly, they are not offering us peace. We must not be angry with our brothers who are like an older brother, entitled to be angry with us at this moment. But we know our lives better, and we know what the Muslims and Croats are offering us in a community with them. They turned us into Turks and converted us to their religion, they impaled us, they gouged out our eyes. We want our own house, around which the winds will play freely, and we shall live freely in that house of ours. We can do that, brothers and sisters, and we have won that right and we are Orthodox, Serbian Orthodox and justice is on our side. Thank you. And good luck."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I'll just confirm quickly before I move on, in the interests of time, that was you speaking; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I may return to that if there is time, but in the interest of concluding, I want to move next to the subject of the Presidency and something you discussed during your examination-in-chief. You were asked about the notion of an Extended Presidency and what that meant to you. In fairness to you, before I proceed, I want to indicate that the subject about which I'm speaking has been referred to variously as the Extended Presidency or Expanded Presidency or War Presidency, so I want to know if, in light of any of those terms, it changes your answers about your awareness of that body in 1992.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency can exist only if a state of war has been declared. I asked that this be done. A state of war was declared in April, and had the War Presidency decided that, there would have been no Assembly then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, what you're saying, Mr. Kasagic, is that a War Presidency can exist legally, or under the constitution, only if a state of war has been declared, but obviously a body such as that can exist in reality, irrespective of any declaration; correct? It can simply be formed even though it doesn't necessarily satisfy, in a punctilious way, the legal requirement. It's just a matter of logic; right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it does not have legal significance. It was not legally significant. It decided on nothing. The Assembly made decisions. The Assembly was significant. And had there been a War Presidency, then there would have been no Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that you are a self-declared legalist, and I see that you're pointing us to, again, the legal significance. But let me turn now to the reality of the situation in 1992, including a reality that was made known to the members of the Assembly, including yourself. First of all, as a preliminary matter, I think we can agree that you never attended any sessions of the Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during 1992, I take it you did not review any minutes of the sessions of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall reviewing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know that before the 31st of May, when Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Djeric attended Presidency sessions, there was a clear distinction between the members of the Presidency and those two as people in attendance, and after June 1st the minutes referred to them as members of the Presidency. You didn't know that, did you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't know that the minutes of the Presidency also contain an explicit reference to the Presidency in expanded composition. That's something else you weren't aware of; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if the witness has not reviewed them, he seems to have no knowledge whatever about it, I wonder whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It does seem to run afoul of the Court's earlier guidance and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me move then to something you do know about, and that's the discussion of this issue at the November 1992 session of the Assembly held in Zvornik. That's the 22nd Session of the Assembly. Now, at that session, the subject of whether or not the War Presidency should continue was a topic of discussion. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that Assembly session, I remember what I said, and I think that Mr. Karadzic was elected president of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, and there were two vice-presidents; Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic. It was a three-member Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's keep our eye on the ball for a moment, because my question focussed on the discussion concerning the continued existence of the War Presidency. And in that connection, let me remind you about the comments made by Mr. Trbojevic and Dr. Karadzic at that session. First of all, Mr. Trbojevic raised the issue and said that: "First of all, we have set up a para-system of power, the public and so-called legal 'war state Presidency' is a body that doesn't exist in the constitution." Okay. So that issue was before the Assembly. Do you remember Mr. Trbojevic's comments or not?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then Dr. Karadzic responded, and he said: "I was all in favour of the Presidency, instead of a president, because there's a lot of work to be done, and if Mr. Koljevic and I are busy, we have Biljana, and even if she's busy, then we have Mr. Krajisnik. We've never come into conflict in the Presidency, without me or any of us being ready to give in. We put all ideas on the table, discuss them, and when we decide which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one of us is the best, we go on." Do you remember those comments?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember the discussion at all, only my contribution to the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Maksimovic and Mr. Jokanovic both referring to the fact that they had been appointed as commissioners by the War Presidency of Republika Srpska? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, although I appreciate the fact that the witness isn't aware of it, I would refer the Court to the minutes of the Presidency session on 30 November 1992, which concluded that -- which directed itself to a discussion of the War Presidencies and the expanded or republic level War Presidency and said: "If these institutions are retained, then the constitution must be amended."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kasagic, I recognise there's a great deal that you don't recall, but maybe this is an issue that comes close enough to some of your responsibilities that you may recall this in connection with the War Presidency. And in that connection, I refer you to the 20th Session of the Assembly, held in September 1992, during which there was reference to the constitutional commission, or constitutional issues committee. You were a member of that committee; right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I was a member of the constitutional commission, or rather, I was a member of the constitutional commission.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall the members of that commission in 1992, and specifically, the people who were elected or re-elected in September of 1992? And if you don't, I can repeat their names for you.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only recall the name of Slobodan Bijelic. I don't recall any others. Of him, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: According to the minutes of that session, the following people were members of that session -- members of that commission, elected or re-elected at that session. The chairman was Mr. Krajisnik; the deputy chairman was Mr. Cancar; and the members included Mr. Maksimovic, Mr. Bijelic, as you noted, yourself, Mr. Spremo, Mr. Trbojevic, Mr. Kalinic, Mr. Buha, Mr. Pejovic, and Mr. Milanovic. Now, does that conform, first of all, with your recollection of the membership of the commission?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of some of them, Milanovic, yes; Maksimovic, yes; Trbojevic, I recall him very little. The ones I remember best are Slobodan Bijelic and now Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at that session, Mr. Krajisnik said -- talking about the commissions, and he said: "We asked the constitutional commission to include a government and a Presidency member, and that was how the commission was formed." Okay. So the commission was to include a Presidency member and a government member. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the Assembly transcript indicates such. Now, the members of government who were on the commission included Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Kalinic; correct? They were members of government?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milanovic, Mr. Pejovic, Mr. Buha, Mr. Kalinic, Mr. Trbojevic too, Mr. Spremo, yourself, Mr. Bijelic, Mr. Maksimovic, Mr. Cancar, none of those were members of the Presidency, were they?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was Mr. Krajisnik who was the member of the Presidency who was included on the Presidency commission, as was ordained; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Assembly. As for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, is your testimony that you have no recollection that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of this constitutional commission? Because you mentioned a lot of the others that came back into your mind now. You did not mention Mr. Krajisnik. Now you're specifically asked whether Mr. Krajisnik, as a Presidency member - that's the question by Mr. Tieger - and then you said: No, he was chairman of the Assembly. Was he a member of that committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know he was a member of the commission when I was a member of the commission. Whether it was in that year, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It takes us again quite some time to get to what seems perhaps an important point. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, you told us earlier about what you learned in 1992 about crimes committed against Muslims and Croats in general, and specifically, in Keraterm, in Prijedor. I want to turn your attention then to the next exhibit, which is number -- in tab 40. Before I do, let me ask you, Mr. -- with them, I'll turn you to tab 40 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that needs an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P999, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P999, Mr. Kasagic, is a SRNA article from 21 January 1996, at the time you were Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, shortly after the Srebrenica massacre. And it reflects, Mr. Kasagic, your denial of claims by Muslims and by international circles about alleged crimes against Muslims in the area of Srebrenica and Prijedor: "He said that there was no evidence for such claims." Mr. Kasagic, it's true that you denied, in 1996, that there was any evidence for crimes against Muslims in Srebrenica and in Prijedor; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard over Radio Banja Luka, that I denied that, but I actually never denied it. I actually told Slobodan Milosevic that a crime had been committed in Srebrenica, because Elizabeth Wren had been in the area and had noticed some dead bodies of young men in the woods there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you point to any public statement in which you, as Prime Minister of Republika Srpska, acknowledged the Srebrenica massacre at or shortly after, or at any time in the general time frame that they occurred, and when the international outcry took place?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Leighton Smith, an admiral of the British navy, sought the support of the government to go and search the area. I agreed and I said, If you need a police escort, police support, that's fine. And he said that they didn't need it, and he went to the area to investigate it. He didn't tell me what he found.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue this too far, in light of the time, but that's quite a different thing; cooperating with international community demands for access to the area is quite a different thing from a governmental cover-up and broad-based denial that such crimes took place. Isn't it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger -- of course I will give you an opportunity to -- the witness -- you confront him with what seems to be a press publication. The witness denied that he made such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask a foundational question, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Isn't it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse -- I told Mr. Josse that he would have an opportunity. Does it cover more or less the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. Simply this: The previous question was about a broad-based denial. It wasn't about a governmental cover-up. That's really taking the matter rather further, but no doubt my learned friend will deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, isn't it correct that the article before us now, from SRNA, reflected the official reaction and position of the government of Republika Srpska until very recently? My question concerns the last paragraph of that article, in which you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to object. What's the point of that question, with respect? If it relates to the witness, I understand, but generally about the government of Republika Srpska up to today, how does that help, I submit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm asking the Prime Minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got no objection if it relates to him at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So "until very recently" is at the time. Yes. Could you tell us whether this reflects the official reaction you gave at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My official reaction was that I did not know about that, that I heard from representatives of the international community that there had been crimes. And I could not say that there hadn't been any crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question is not whether you could have said it. The question is whether you said it. But I do understand from your answer that this article does not reflect your words that you did not deny that it took place, but you just didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't deny it. I did not deny it. I didn't know. I didn't know, and I couldn't deny it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes if people do not know things, they nevertheless deny it. But that's a theoretical part. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the article indicates that you said there was no evidence for such claims. Is that what you're saying now, that at the time you didn't know whether there was such evidence, and that's the statement you issued?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know, and I never challenged it, the crimes of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to your question, Mr. Tieger. [Inaudible] ... the witness still thinks now that there's no evidence. Please, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that what you were saying at the time, that as far as you knew, there was no evidence for such claims about crimes in Srebrenica and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said at all that there wasn't any evidence. I did not say that there wasn't any evidence about Prijedor. I had heard that there had been some killings, and I cannot say, as far as Srebrenica is concerned, when I heard about some crimes having been committed, that I denied that they were committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Tieger, on -- I don't dare to mention the page, because I was interrupted for a short moment, but when I said that's not an answer to your question, Mr. Tieger, and then the witness still thinks now that there's no evidence, that's not -- that does not reflect what I said. I said that your question was whether the witness now still thinks that there's no evidence. That's different from what appears on the transcript. And it's a sensitive issue, so therefore I correct it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you say in 1995, Mr. Kasagic, after the indictment of Radovan Karadzic and General Mladic, that a trial of those two would amount to a trial of the entire Serbian people for alleged crimes?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that I said that the trial of the top people of a nation is a trial of that nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that regard, I would refer the Court to tab 36. That will need an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 36, Your Honours, will be P1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that article reflects the comment to which we just referred; right? That would be at the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. Well, I don't know whether those were my exact words or not. I don't know whether I said every one of these words, but that was the way I was thinking. I don't know if I said the word "vicious."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber needs five minutes for a procedural issue still. I take it that you are about to finish your cross-examination. At the same time, I do not know whether Mr. Josse has -- whether there's any need to re-examine the witness, because he would have to stay if --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have instructions to re-examine quite extensively. Could I speak to Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. And at the same time, you are sufficiently experienced to assess the present situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't wasted the Court's time. There's one issue that I've been asked to re-examine on, out of quite a number. It won't take very long. That's what I'm requesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have just two matters to raise, Your Honour, which I thought would take about ten minutes. It was my estimate before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then how much time would you need, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, for that one issue, shall we say five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now addressing the interpreters and the technicians: That would mean that approximately we would need another 15 minutes. I would need five minutes for a procedural issue. The Chamber has no further questions, at least as it stands now. Would it be possible, because for the Bench it would be difficult to resume later this day. We have considered that before, but there is a problem, a practical problem. Would it be possible to continue for another -- yes, I see -- thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Tieger, you have ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, although you've come here and tried to present Mr. Krajisnik as essentially the equivalent of you, just another deputy, the fact of the matter is that outside of Court, on other occasions, you've been comfortable referring to him as a leader; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people accepted him as a leader. The people loved him. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A leader in a key position, with all the power that that entailed; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about whether he was in a key position or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just direct your attention to two passages and then we'll conclude. The first are remarks that you made at the 50th Assembly Session. That's found at tab 34. And I believe in the version before you, Mr. Kasagic, that's found at 00845889. And on that occasion, you said: "The hardest job, in my opinion, is done by those who are in the trenches and those who are in the key positions, in the highest political posts. I do not mean that I am one of them. I mean those who are at the highest level. For example, I look at my friend Momo from a distance. Three years ago he had a few grey hairs and now I see he is completely grey." That was a reference in the Assembly to Mr. Krajisnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it looks, that it was a reference to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, I want to direct your attention to a couple of comments you made during your interview in 2001. First of all, it's a minor matter on page 40, beginning at line 24, when asked about visits by Mr. Krajisnik to Banja Luka, you said: "If he would be coming, he'd be coming together with Radovan Karadzic. They would usually be coming together." But more to the point we're talking about now, I'd like to turn your attention to a passage at page 43, where you were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you haven't mentioned the tab in which we have to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, it's page 43 at tab 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were asked: "Who was responsible for that kind of fear that existed that would cause people to give up everything they owned to move to another country?" And you began by saying: "There was a strong propaganda drive and that instilled this fear into the people." And then you continued to the part that is pertinent to us at the moment: "It was all part of a propaganda effort and campaign which was designed with the idea to instil fear into people. Unfortunately, leading politicians in these parts were people who had prison term record. Tudjman and Izetbegovic, because of their national, nationalistic views, Krajisnik and Karadzic because of economic crime. They all wanted to be kings of their own small little areas and you could achieve that only by launching a propaganda campaign and lies." Those were your comments in 2001, isn't that right, Mr. Kasagic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at that time, I didn't have the information that the proceedings against Karadzic and Krajisnik had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that that's not the core of your question, but that it was not a reference to the prison term record, but on what had happened, rather than whether the people that you mentioned had ever been in prison. Is that correct, Mr. Tieger, that that was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So forget about whether there was any incorrectness, but apart from the new knowledge you have on the proceedings against Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic, apart from that, is this what your comment was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was my knowledge and that means that that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, there was one matter you wanted to raise with the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, somewhat earlier you said that you learned various things at the sessions of the Assembly, that you weren't the only one who knew about that; all the representatives of the Serbian Republic knew about it. And you were referring to the forcible expulsion of Muslims and Croats. When you were talking in that context about forcible expulsions of Muslims and Croats, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that there was a war on and that everybody's afraid of the war. The economy could not function. People remained jobless. And that there were expulsions from apartments, forcible expulsions. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how was this information disseminated around the Assembly members?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports about unemployment, poverty. I think that that was the way it was. I even attacked the government once on account of that, because I had information that a mother was feeding her child with bread from warm water [as interpreted]. So I attacked the government on account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me grasp the nettle, Mr. Kasagic. Does forcible expulsions - using that term - amount to ethnic cleansing? Are they one and the same?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serbs were being expelled, and that can be understood as ethnic cleansing, but together with the Serbs, due to economic reasons. Ethnic cleansing is having people expelled from apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question. Is it really your testimony that ethnic cleansing, that you understand that to be removing persons from their apartments for economic reasons? Is that really your testimony, Kasagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Economic reasons are one reason, and expulsion from apartments is another thing. So a person who has no apartment has to go somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you'd say if you, as you said before, if you have to remove someone from the territory of the area, of course the first step is to get him out of his apartment, but that's not a complete expulsion, in your view, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's hard for me to condemn that. A court can condemn that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you condemned it or not. But we're just trying to find out what you understand by "forcibly expelling people." And you gave, for one moment, the impression to me that you thought expulsion to be completed if you had taken someone out of his apartment. I'm asking whether expulsion is completed by that act, or that it would need more to talk about forcible expulsion from areas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not sufficient if they have some other place to stay. Several families would stay in one apartment, but then if they were all expelled from that apartment, then that is forcible expulsion, because they have nowhere else to go, or stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me put the question quite simply to you: When you earlier told about what you learned in the Assembly about forcibly expelling people, was it about putting them before the front door of their apartments, so that they had to stay in a park, or was it that they were moved out from the territory of the relevant village, municipality, wherever the place where they used to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Gornji Vakuf, I saw that they were relocated, one group. I think they were Muslims, but I don't know whether they were both Croats and Muslims. I saw that it was forcibly relocated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why don't you answer my question? I talked -- you gave earlier as your sources what you learnt in the Assembly and what you saw with your own eyes. I referred you to what you learned in the Assembly, when they are talking about -- when you learned there that people were forcibly expelled, did you say that they end up in the park in front of their house or in the meadow in front of their house, or was it your understanding that forcible expulsion meant that they were driven out from the village, municipality, where they used to live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expelled from their apartments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, any further questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. Our position is that there were some other areas of re-examination, but in the interests of this witness returning, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. I'll just reread a portion of the transcript of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you earlier were speaking, Mr. Kasagic, about forcible expulsion, and also about the fact that the international community would not accept forcible expulsion for Banja Luka, you said: "The international community would not allow that kind of attitude towards these people. It would be a column from Banja Luka all the way up to Gradiska." But I do understand that forcible expulsion, for you, is taking him out of his apartment, leaving him in front of his apartment, and that's it, or perhaps relocate him to the next street. But when you were talking about forcible expulsion, you explained that, that that would mean a column from Banja Luka all the way up to Gradiska. That's approximately 50 kilometres, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was responding to what people said about Muslims and Croats living in Banja Luka. I said you can't compare life in a small village with life in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because expelling them would mean a column of taking them 50 kilometres from where they used to live, isn't it? And isn't Gradiska at the border of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest to you, I have some difficulties in reconciling the way you spoke about expulsions and the definition you later gave to us. If there would be anything you would like to add to that in order to make me better understand this discrepancy, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I felt they could not be expelled. There was no such column. However, evicting someone from an apartment means depriving them of the conditions necessary for life. Ethnic cleansing would be for all Muslims and Croats to move away from Banja Luka and go to live in Croatia, or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what about the measure -- or the situation being only temporary, that people would later return? Was this to say that they would return from the street, the next street, and then return to their apartments? Is that how I have to understand the return after the war?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They left the Republika Srpska because they had no place to live. When the war was ended, they came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So do I then understand your testimony rightly to say that expelling someone is taking him out of his apartment, then he leaves voluntarily and leaves the territory of the Republic, and that that's all voluntary, and apart from that, of course, they have been evicted from their apartment? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely, because he has nowhere to live if he doesn't have the conditions to live because he has no apartment, then he has to leave. So in a way, his leaving is forced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. No further questions? The Chamber has no further questions either. Mr. Kasagic, I'd like to thank you very much for having come a long way to The Hague and to answer the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Kasagic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you asked for further guidance in view of scheduling. Perhaps it will assist you if you would first listen to an amendment to the April 2005 scheduling order. This statement I'm giving now constitutes an amendment to the scheduling order of the Chamber of the 26th of April, 2005. You will recall that that scheduling order was already amended once, allowing the Defence to commence presentation of its case on the 10th of October, 2005, instead of on the 12th of September, 2005. Since the commencement of the Defence case, counsel for the Defence has urged the Chamber to grant the Defence additional time in preparation, which means effectively additional time in which the Defence may present its case. The current deadline for the conclusion of the Defence case is the 10th of March, 2006. The April 2005 scheduling order provided that a deadline could be extended upon a showing of, I quote, "good cause" by one of the parties. The reality is that the Defence is already experiencing considerable scheduling difficulties, and I'll just indicate some of them. There have been significant forced gaps in the sitting schedule to date. There is an inability to plan witnesses beyond the very short term. The Rule 65 ter summaries are mostly insufficient or seriously deficient. A trimmed list of Defence witnesses has not been forthcoming. The time estimates for examination-in-chief seem to be mere guesses, not based on prior interviews with witnesses. Most of the material to be exhibited is produced in the eleventh hour, and moreover, it is mostly untranslated. Expert witnesses have not been identified. Rule 92 bis evidence has yet to be collected, subject to the formalities. And counsel for the Defence has expressed unwillingness or inability to commit himself to closing the Defence case by certain dates. This is a reality that is causing the Chamber great concern. We have no doubt that both parties, including Mr. Krajisnik, feel the same way. The Chamber does understand that the dispute with the Registry concerning finances has been settled by an agreement. Mr. Josse, I'm not saying whether it's the agreement the Defence would have wished, but at least it's settled by an agreement. The assessment of the contribution Mr. Krajisnik has to make to his Defence has not been affected by that agreement. Yet, good cause or not, we have decided to grant the Defence an extra seven weeks to prepare and present its case. This means that the Defence case must close by the 28th of April, 2006. All other dates shown in the April 2005 order are pushed back by seven weeks. Good cause continues to be a condition for any extension of those dates. However, the Defence case shall not be further extended unless exceptional circumstances can be demonstrated. This is a higher standard than good cause. This concludes the Chamber's amendment to its April 2005 scheduling order. The Chamber now wishes to explain certain matters to the parties, and especially to the Defence. Trials in the context of this Tribunal have several peculiar features. One is an oversupply of potentially relevant witnesses. This is especially true of the present case, which concerns events in a large part of Bosnia and Herzegovina which occurred over a period of many months. In the pre-trial phase, the Prosecution's case was heavily trimmed by the Chamber. It was further trimmed in the course of the trial. Lastly, the Prosecution was ordered to wrap up its case by the 22nd of July of this year. In effect, the Prosecution was limited to calling those persons whom it considered its most highly relevant witnesses. There is a public interest in giving the Prosecution sufficient time and resources to prosecute those suspected of having committed crimes, just as there is a public interest -- of course apart from the private interest, there's a public interest in giving every accused person sufficient time and resources to defend himself or herself. The Chamber must ensure a fair contest, subject to the constraint of an expeditious trial, which is another public interest. It follows that the Defence, like the Prosecution, is expected to line up the most highly relevant witnesses for its case and present as much of their evidence as it can in the course of an allotted period of time. It is not an open-ended quest. In normal circumstances, where the requirements of Rule 65 ter (G) have been adequately fulfilled by the Defence, the Chamber is in the position to determine the number of witnesses the Defence may call, and if necessary, to shorten the estimated examination time for each witness. I'm here referring to Rule 63 ter, subparagraphs B and C. This gives the Chamber the capacity to plan and maintain control of the proceedings. Because the Defence fails to provide the Chamber with the necessary information to properly make the Rule 73 ter determinations, we are opting instead for giving the Defence a fixed period of time in which to call its most highly relevant witnesses. It's largely to the Defence to decide how best to use the time between now and the 28th of April to prepare and to present its case. The Chamber is aware, and the parties should be aware as well, that the lack of a well-developed schedule for the presentation of the Defence case may have its impact on future developments. The Chamber may find it difficult in the future to establish that sufficient reasons exist to deviate from the schedule as it is set now, since the logical point of reference, which is comparison with the fully developed schedule that was initially presented, is not available, and therefore, the Chamber will have to rely on its own assessment underlying the present new scheduling order to consider whether there are any good reasons to amend the schedule. I would like to draw the attention of the Defence to the likelihood that if it continues the presentation of its case at the current pace, that by the end of April 2006, it will have managed to present no more than 40 witnesses, including the evidence of Mr. Krajisnik. This is many fewer witnesses than indicated in the Defence Rule 65 ter (G) listing. If the Defence is interested in the arithmetic underlying the Chamber's calculations, an explanatory sheet, together with a colour-coded calendar, may be obtained from Mr. Registrar at the end of this session. As for short-term scheduling, the Chamber has decided to grant the Defence's request for an adjournment commencing on the 24th and 25th of November, depending on when next week's witnesses are concluded. Hearings will resume on the -- it says on the 5th of December -- yes, on the 5th of December, for two weeks. Then the winter recess follows, with hearings to restart on -- it says Wednesday, the 11th of January, although I have to add to that that only hours ago, the Chamber received a request not to schedule any sitting in the week of the 9th of January until the 13th of January. So therefore, that perhaps has to be reconsidered. It has got something to do with courtrooms being under reconstruction and not all courtrooms being available. So that may change. After that week, at least, we would not be sitting in the week -- Mr. Krajisnik's testimony is said to commence on Monday, the 23rd of January, 2006, and after Mr. Krajisnik's testimony, the programme is still unknown to the Chamber. The Defence is ordered to specify its programme of witnesses and desired non-sitting days at least two weeks in advance, and this is an ongoing obligation. As for expert witnesses, the Defence is ordered to announce whether it will call experts, and if so, who they will be, by the 13th of January, 2006. Tuesday, the 28th of February, 2006 is the deadline for filing any expert reports. Finally, the Chamber emphasises that its responsibilities and duties under Rule 90(F) is not affected in any way by the new schedule and that the Chamber will closely follow the development of the presentation of the Defence case. I would like to add to this that the short-term scheduling, as I just gave it, exists merely in following what the Defence had expressed as its wish during the conversations with the legal officer. To that extent, it also expresses the view of the Chamber now, that the Defence organises its case as it wishes, of course within certain limits, but that the 28th of April is a date which is not easily to be amended. The Chamber is not in a position, due to the absence of any commitment or any well-completed, long-term scheduling, to sensibly assist the Defence in a better organisation of the presentation of its case by giving directives of a different character than just pointing at the 28th of April. This concludes the Chamber's remarks on the schedule. Is this sufficient, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Clearly, Mr. Stewart and I will consider Your Honour's words very carefully. And the only other comment I've got is in relation to Tuesday. During the course of the morning, a further Court calendar, official Court calendar, was produced, and I note that we're still due to sit on Tuesday morning. Can I confirm that we are definitely going to sit on Tuesday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check that. From what I understood, it was only recently changed, and therefore, it might not appear yet in the Court schedule. I'll verify that first of all, and then you can contact Mr. Nilsson, the legal officer, for information. It's a matter of 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Two other very brief matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The protected witness application, Your Honour, I don't know whether that's something that Your Honour wishes to hear any oral argument about on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the parties are expected to see whether they can agree on protective measures, yes or no. If there is an agreement, then of course we just get the application, we get the reasons for it, we get a response from the Prosecution. Then it's easily dealt with without any oral argument. If not, then of course we'd like to hear that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally, this: Again it's a matter that I'll liaise with Mr. Tieger about, but there may be some observations and submissions I wish to make about his cross-examination today, but let me speak to him first, if I may, Your Honour. But I reserve the right to return to that subject. Clearly, there wasn't time to deal with it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if that doesn't lead to any common understanding, we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further matters that I wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. I again would like to apologise to the interpreters and technicians, because again it was 15 minutes earlier, but at least Mr. Kasagic can travel home again. Therefore, thank you very much and I hope that you will better enjoy your weekend. We'll adjourn until next Monday morning, Courtroom III, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of November 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 25
